item.title: The Birth of Venus
item.lesson: A thousand years after the fall of Rome, a life-size nude goddess returned to Western painting. Botticelli, working in the orbit of the Medici family and their humanist circle, painted the goddess of love arriving at shore on a shell, blown in by the wind god Zephyr and welcomed by a nymph holding a flowered cloak. Her pose is borrowed directly from ancient 'Venus Pudica' statues — the Medici owned one — making the painting a deliberate handshake between pagan antiquity and Renaissance Florence. That embrace of mythology was daring: within a decade, the preacher Savonarola would have Florentines burning 'pagan' luxuries, and Botticelli's style would fall so far from fashion that he died obscure. The painting waited in Medici villas for centuries before the world decided it was one of the most beloved images ever made.
item.lookFor: Botticelli was a supreme draftsman of line: trace the impossible, lovely anatomy — the neck too long, the shoulder sloping like water — that makes Venus float rather than stand.
